PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 53 — Lesson 77: Geriatric Assessment

FNP-level goal: Assess the older adult through function, cognition, mobility, medications, goals, social context, and physiology—not chronological age alone. Recognize frailty, falls, delirium, medication-related harm, orthostatic symptoms, caregiver strain, elder mistreatment, and acute decline that must not be dismissed as “normal aging.”

Learning Objectives

  • Use a comprehensive geriatric framework that integrates medical conditions with function, cognition, mobility, medications, nutrition, mood, sensory ability, and social support.
  • Evaluate falls and dizziness by reconstructing the event and identifying cardiovascular, neurologic, medication, sensory, environmental, and musculoskeletal contributors.
  • Distinguish delirium from chronic cognitive impairment and depression, and recognize delirium as a medical emergency until evaluated.
  • Perform a high-yield medication reconciliation that includes prescription, OTC, supplement, alcohol, and nonprescribed products.
  • Screen for frailty, malnutrition, functional loss, caregiver burden, and possible elder mistreatment using a trauma-informed approach.
  • Build safe, goal-concordant outpatient plans with clear escalation, interdisciplinary referral, and closed-loop follow-up.

Part 1 — Aging Is Heterogeneous; Function Is Clinical Data

Older adults vary greatly in physiologic reserve, functional ability, chronic disease burden, cognition, social support, and goals. Begin by asking what the person could do before this change and what they can do now. Assess activities of daily living (bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, feeding) and instrumental activities (medications, finances, meals, transportation, shopping, technology, and household tasks). A new decline in function may be the earliest sign of infection, heart failure, stroke, medication toxicity, depression, pain, malnutrition, or unsafe living conditions.

Use age-appropriate vital signs, weight trend, orthostatic measurements when indicated, appearance, gait, cognition, sensory function, mood, nutrition, and medication review. “They are just old” is never an acceptable diagnostic explanation for confusion, fall, weight loss, weakness, new incontinence, fatigue, or loss of independence.

Part 2 — Frailty: Reduced Reserve Changes Risk

Frailty is a state of increased vulnerability to stressors because physiologic reserve and resilience are reduced. Clues may include unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow gait, low activity, recurrent falls, reduced grip/transfer strength, and difficulty recovering from a minor illness. Frailty is not synonymous with age, disability, or a diagnosis; it changes how an acute illness, medication change, hospitalization, and procedure may affect the patient.

When frailty is suspected, evaluate reversible contributors: inadequate intake, dental/oral problems, depression, sleep, pain, anemia, thyroid/endocrine disease, heart/lung/kidney disease, infection, medication effects, social isolation, food insecurity, and deconditioning. Align interventions with patient priorities, prognostic context, and caregiver capacity. A narrow disease-by-disease plan can fail if it ignores function and feasibility.

Part 3 — Falls: A Symptom and a Sentinel Event

A fall is not simply an accident. Reconstruct the event: what happened immediately before, during, and after; location/time; position change; prodrome such as dizziness, palpitations, chest symptoms, weakness, or visual change; loss of consciousness; head strike; injury; footwear; assistive device; environmental hazard; and ability to get up. Ask about prior falls, fear of falling, near-falls, gait change, urgency/nocturia, alcohol, and medication timing.

Possible contributors include orthostatic hypotension, arrhythmia/syncope, stroke/TIA, seizure, hypoglycemia, infection, dehydration, neuropathy, Parkinsonism, vestibular disease, vision/hearing impairment, arthritis, foot pain, sarcopenia, anemia, and medication effects. A fall after standing should prompt orthostatic assessment and medication review; a fall with head injury, anticoagulant use, loss of consciousness, focal deficit, persistent vomiting, severe pain, or inability to bear weight may require emergency evaluation.

Part 4 — Mobility and Examination

Observe transfers, gait speed, turning, balance, footwear, use of assistive devices, posture, tremor, range of motion, foot skin/deformity, pulses, sensation, strength, and pain. When safe and within competence, structured tools such as Timed Up and Go, chair-stand, or balance assessment can support a broader mobility evaluation. Do not test an unstable patient without assistance or treat a single test result as the diagnosis.

Mobility recommendations often require an interdisciplinary plan: physical therapy, occupational therapy, home-safety assessment, vision/hearing care, podiatry, pharmacy collaboration, nutrition support, and caregiver education. The FNP’s role includes connecting the medical mechanism with realistic interventions and confirming access.

Part 5 — Delirium: Acute Change Is a Medical Emergency

Delirium is an acute disturbance in attention and awareness that often fluctuates. It may appear as agitation, hallucinations, sleep-wake reversal, withdrawal, inattention, slowed responses, or a “quiet” loss of engagement. Establish baseline cognition and the time course using caregivers or facility staff when permitted. New confusion in an older adult is delirium until a medical evaluation identifies the cause.

Common contributors include infection, hypoxia, dehydration, pain, constipation, urinary retention, metabolic/endocrine disturbance, medication toxicity or withdrawal, alcohol/substance exposure, stroke, seizure, trauma, and environmental change. A normal-looking urine test or a known dementia diagnosis does not end the differential. Delirium with unstable vital signs, focal neurologic symptoms, trauma, severe agitation, inability to take medications/fluids, or unsafe supervision requires urgent/emergency care.

Part 6 — Cognition, Depression, and Capacity

Chronic cognitive impairment typically has a slower course than delirium, but baseline decline still requires functional assessment, safety review, caregiver input, medication review, depression screening, sensory assessment, and evaluation for reversible contributors. Ask about finances, driving, medications, cooking, wandering, firearms/other safety issues as appropriate, and caregiver strain. Cognitive screening tools can support assessment but do not replace history, examination, collateral information, and longitudinal observation.

Depression can present with low energy, appetite/weight change, poor concentration, sleep change, somatic symptoms, and reduced participation. It may mimic or coexist with cognitive disorder. Decision-making capacity is specific to the decision and can fluctuate; do not equate a diagnosis of dementia, advanced age, language difference, or an “unwise” choice with lack of capacity. Follow local legal and institutional processes when capacity is in question.

Part 7 — Polypharmacy and Medication-Related Harm

Medication reconciliation must include every prescription, OTC product, vitamin, supplement, herbal product, topical, inhaler, injection, alcohol, and nonprescribed substance—plus dose, schedule, indication, prescriber, actual use, recent changes, affordability, and side effects. Multiple medications, kidney/liver change, altered body composition, cognitive impairment, and fragmented prescribers increase the chance of adverse effects and interactions.

Medications for sleep, anxiety, pain, blood pressure, mood, seizures, bladder symptoms, and other conditions may contribute to dizziness, sedation, slowed reaction time, visual change, hypotension, falls, and cognitive symptoms. Do not stop essential drugs abruptly or make a blanket “deprescribe everything” plan. Use structured medication review, clarify current indications and goals, assess benefit versus harm, coordinate with prescribers/pharmacists, and monitor any planned change.

Part 8 — Orthostasis, Syncope, and Dizziness

Dizziness is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Ask whether the patient means spinning, lightheadedness, imbalance, weakness, presyncope, or nonspecific disequilibrium. Relate symptoms to position change, exertion, meals, medication timing, hydration, palpitations, neurologic signs, hearing symptoms, and falls. Measure orthostatic vital signs when indicated and interpret them in the patient’s broader hemodynamic and medication context.

Chest pain, palpitations, exertional syncope, new focal neurologic symptoms, severe headache, persistent vomiting, active bleeding/anemia concern, abnormal vital signs, or injury after a fall requires urgent evaluation. Do not call recurrent presyncope “vertigo” without a cardiovascular and medication differential.

Part 9 — Nutrition, Sensory Loss, and Social Context

Ask about unintentional weight loss, appetite, chewing/swallowing, dentition, nausea, constipation, food availability, meal preparation, income, isolation, alcohol, and ability to shop/cook. Assess vision and hearing because small changes can affect falls, medication use, communication, cognition testing, mood, and safety. Address hearing aids, glasses, lighting, footwear, home hazards, transportation, and literacy as practical clinical interventions.

Screen privately and respectfully for elder mistreatment, neglect, exploitation, caregiver burnout, and unsafe living conditions when clinically indicated. Document objective concerns and follow mandatory-reporting, social-work, and institutional processes. Supportive questions are safer and more useful than accusatory confrontation.

Part 10 — Goals of Care and Diagnostic Proportionality

High-quality geriatric care is not doing less; it is doing what is most likely to help the individual patient. Ask about goals, function, symptom burden, acceptable tradeoffs, who helps with decisions, advance directives, and preferred setting of care. Testing and treatment should be clinically indicated and consistent with patient values, anticipated benefit, burden, life expectancy, and access.

Shared decision-making does not mean offering every possible test without guidance. Explain what each option can and cannot accomplish, assess decisional capacity for the choice at hand, include a surrogate when legally appropriate, and document the plan. Acute instability still requires emergency action regardless of chronic goals-of-care discussions.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: Fall After Standing

An 82-year-old falls when rising from bed at night. They report lightheadedness, take several medications, have nocturia, and have had two near-falls in the last month.

FNP reasoning: reconstruct the fall; assess injury, orthostatic physiology, medication timing, hydration, vision, gait, home environment, and cardiac/neuro red flags. A fall after standing is not automatically “clumsiness” and should trigger an individualized multifactorial prevention plan.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: New Confusion

An 86-year-old with stable mild memory impairment becomes inattentive, sleepy, and intermittently agitated over one day after a new medication and poor fluid intake.

FNP reasoning: acute fluctuation from baseline suggests delirium. Evaluate for medical causes and safety immediately; do not assume this is expected progression of dementia.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Weight Loss and Medication Burden

A 78-year-old has unintentional weight loss, fatigue, dizziness, and difficulty organizing twelve daily medications. They have had no recent medication reconciliation and live alone.

FNP reasoning: assess nutrition, depression, medical causes, cognition/function, falls risk, and every medication’s indication/actual use. Build a coordinated plan with pharmacy, family/supports when appropriate, and follow-up rather than adding another prescription without understanding the regimen.

FNP Geriatric Assessment Framework

  1. Begin with baseline and function: what changed in ADLs/IADLs, mobility, cognition, intake, and social support?
  2. Assess acute danger: injury, syncope, delirium, stroke/ACS signs, infection/sepsis, dehydration, medication toxicity, and ability to remain safe.
  3. Reconstruct falls and dizziness: event details, orthostasis, cardiac/neuro symptoms, gait/sensory factors, home environment, and medications.
  4. Distinguish delirium: acute fluctuating inattention/awareness is medical until evaluated.
  5. Reconcile all medications: indication, dose, actual use, duplicate products, prescribers, interactions, adverse effects, and affordability.
  6. Assess goals and supports: nutrition, sensory needs, caregiver capacity, safety, transportation, health literacy, advance-care preferences, and social work/community linkage.
  7. Close the loop: concrete follow-up, medication-change monitoring, PT/OT/pharmacy/referral access, result ownership, and emergency precautions.

High-Yield Summary

Function: new loss of independence is clinical data and can be the first sign of acute illness or medication harm.
Frailty: reduced reserve increases vulnerability; seek reversible contributors and align care with goals.
Falls: reconstruct the event and evaluate orthostatic, cardiac, neurologic, medication, sensory, mobility, and environmental factors.
Delirium: acute fluctuating inattention/awareness is a medical emergency until evaluated.
Polypharmacy: assess actual use, indication, interactions, renal/hepatic context, affordability, and fall/cognitive burden—do not stop medicines indiscriminately.
Geriatric care: use function, goals, caregiver capacity, and feasibility to make the diagnostic and treatment plan safer.
FNP standard: never substitute “normal aging” for careful assessment, safe disposition, and patient-centered follow-up.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Geriatric assessment, medication changes/deprescribing, capacity evaluation, elder-mistreatment reporting, referral, emergency disposition, and follow-up must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
